questions.question: The roads of Rajshahi are wider -----.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence compares roads (plural) in two different cities — Rajshahi and Dhaka.
Since “roads” is plural, we must use “those” to avoid repetition and to match the plural noun.
So the correct structure is:
The roads of Rajshahi are wider than those of Dhaka.
❌ Why others are incorrect:
B. than Dhaka → Incorrect comparison. We are comparing roads, not the city itself.
C. than that of Dhaka → “That” is singular, but “roads” is plural.
D. than Dhaka's roads → Grammatically possible, but in formal comparison structure, “those of” is preferred and more standard in exam grammar.

questions.question: One's finger prints are ---[]
options: different from those of any other person
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
We are talking about fingerprints, which are plural. To compare them correctly with fingerprints of other people, we use “those of” to avoid repeating the word “fingerprints.”
So the correct sentence is:
One's fingerprints are different from those of any other person.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. different from any other person → Grammatically incomplete. We’re comparing fingerprints, not the person.
C. different than any other person → “Different than” is incorrect in formal English; “different from” is correct.
D. differs from another person → Wrong verb form (“differs” should be “are different”), and again, it compares people rather than fingerprints.

questions.question: Select the correct sentence.[]
options: The roads of Dhaka is wider than Khulna
The roads of Dhaka are wider than those of Khulna
The road of Dhaka are wider than those of Khulna
The roads of Dhaka is wider than those of Khulna
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Subject-verb agreement:
“The roads” → plural → verb must be “are” (not “is”).
Comparison of plural nouns:
Comparing roads in two cities → use “those of” to refer to Khulna’s roads.
So the sentence is correctly written as:
The roads of Dhaka are wider than those of Khulna.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. The roads of Dhaka is wider than Khulna → “roads” is plural, so “is” is incorrect; also missing “those of” for comparison.
C. The road of Dhaka are wider than those of Khulna → “road” is singular, but verb “are” is plural → mismatch.
D. The roads of Dhaka is wider than those of Khulna → Verb “is” is incorrect for plural subject “roads.”

questions.question: Which one is correct ?[]
options: The streets of Dhaka are cleaner than Rajshahi
The streets of Dhaka are cleaner than those of Rajshahi
The streets of Dhaka are more cleaner than Rajshahi
The streets of Dhaka are clean than Rajshahi
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
When we compare streets, we must compare them with streets, not with the city itself.
❌ A. “cleaner than Rajshahi” → This compares streets with a city (incorrect comparison).
❌ C. “more cleaner” → Double comparative (wrong). We use either cleaner or more clean, not both.
❌ D. “clean than” → Incorrect comparative form. It should be cleaner than.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: The houses of our village is better than yours
The houses of our village is good than yours
The houses of our village are good than those of yours
The houses of our village are better than those of yours
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Let’s check the grammar step by step:
1️⃣ Subject–Verb Agreement
The subject is houses (plural).
So we must use are, not is.
❌ A and B are wrong because they use is.
2️⃣ Correct Comparative Form
The comparative of good is better, not good than.
❌ B and C are wrong because they use good than.

questions.question: Put correct part of speech in the gap. One, some, any, many, none are ---[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The words one, some, any, many, none do not refer to any specific person or thing.
They give a general or indefinite idea.
Examples:
Some are absent today.
Many were invited.
None was ready.
One should be honest.
Since they refer to people or things in a general way, they are called Indefinite Pronouns.
Why others are wrong:
❌ Personal pronoun → (I, you, he, she, they)
❌ Interrogative pronoun → (who, whom, which, what)
❌ Demonstrative pronoun → (this, that, these, those)

questions.question: "None but Allah can help us". What kind of pronoun is 'None' ?[]
questions.explanation:
Why the others are wrong:
❌ Reflexive → (myself, himself, themselves) – used when the subject and object are the same.
❌ Reciprocal → (each other, one another) – shows mutual action.
❌ Demonstrative → (this, that, these, those) – points to something specific.
Conclusion:
Since “None” refers to no specific person and means no one, it is an Indefinite Pronoun. ✅

questions.question: Which of the following is correct ?[]
options: One of the most favourite fruit is Mango
One of the most favourite fruits is Mango
One of most favourite fruit is Mango
One of my most favourite fruits are Mango
questions.explanation:
❌ A. “fruit” → After one of the most, the noun must be plural → fruits
❌ C. Missing “the” → It should be one of the most
❌ D. “are” → The subject is One, so the verb must be is, not are
✔ B is correct because:
“One” → singular subject → takes is
“fruits” → plural noun after “one of the most”

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: One of the most beautiful girls has come
One of the most beautiful girl has come
One of the most beautiful girls have come
One of the most beautiful girl are come
questions.explanation:
"One of the..." construction:
When you say "one of the [plural noun]", the subject is "one", which is singular.
Therefore, the verb must also be singular: "has", not "have".
Plural noun after "of the":
We say "girls" (plural) because "one of the girls" refers to one among many girls.
Saying "one of the girl" (singular) is incorrect.
Verb agreement:
Singular subject → singular verb: "has come"
Plural subject → plural verb: "have come" (not applicable here because the subject is "one").

questions.question: One of the ----- his ability to lecture.[]
options: greater attribute of a professor is
greatest attributes of a professor are
greatest attributes of a professor is
greatest attribute of a professor is
questions.explanation:
“One of the …” structure:
The phrase “one of the” is singular, because the subject is “one”, even though it refers to something among many.
Therefore, the verb must be singular: “is”, not “are”.
Noun agreement:
After “one of the”, we usually use the plural form if we talk about multiple things to choose from:
“one of the greatest attributes” ✅
But here, we are saying “one of the greatest attribute is his ability…” – it should be singular, so “attribute” fits.
Putting it together:
“One of the greatest attribute of a professor is his ability to lecture.” → Singular subject + singular verb.
✅ Correct sentence: One of the greatest attribute of a professor is his ability to lecture.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence.[]
options: One of the problems are extremely easy to solve.
One of the problem is extremely easy to solve.
One of the problems is extremely easy to solve.
One of the problem's are extremely easy to solve.
questions.explanation:
“One of the …” construction:
The subject is “one”, which is singular.
So, the verb must also be singular → “is”, not “are”.
Noun after “of the”:
We use the plural form because “one of the …” refers to one among many:
“problems” (plural) is correct
“problem” (singular) is incorrect here.
Putting it together:
One of the problems (plural) is (singular verb) extremely easy to solve.
❌ Why the others are wrong:
A → “are” (wrong verb; should be singular)
B → “problem” (wrong; should be plural)
D → “problem's” + “are” (both wrong; apostrophe makes it possessive, and verb is plural)

questions.question: Which of the following sentences is correct ?[]
options: One of my friends are lawyers
One of my friend is a lawyer
One of my friends is a lawyer
One of my friends are a lawyer
questions.explanation:
“One of the …” rule:
The subject is “one”, which is singular, so the verb must be singular → “is”.
Plural verb like “are” is incorrect here.
Plural noun after “of”:
We say “friends” (plural) because “one of my friends” means one out of many friends.
“Friend” (singular) would be wrong in this construction.
Putting it together:
One (singular) of my friends (plural) is (singular verb) a lawyer.
❌ Why the others are wrong:
A → “are” (wrong verb)
B → “friend” (wrong; should be plural)
D → “are” (wrong verb)
Quick trick:
Whenever you see “one of the …”:
Plural noun after “of the” ✅
Singular verb ✅

questions.question: Which one is correct ?[]
options: One of my cousins are a doctor
One of my cousin is a doctor
One of my cousins is a doctor
One of my cousin are a doctor
questions.explanation:
Subject-verb agreement with “one of the …”
“One” is singular → the verb must be singular → “is”.
Plural verb like “are” is incorrect.
Noun after “of”
Use the plural form because it refers to one among many cousins → “cousins”.
Using “cousin” (singular) here is wrong.
Putting it together
One (singular) of my cousins (plural) is (singular verb) a doctor.
❌ Why the others are wrong:
A → “are” (wrong verb)
B → “cousin” (wrong noun form)
D → both noun and verb are wrong

questions.question: Which one is correct ?[]
options: One of my friends lives in Brighton
One of my friend lives in Brighton
One of my friends live in Brighton
One of my friend live in Brighton
questions.explanation:
“One of the …” structure
The subject is “one” → singular.
So the verb must also be singular → “lives”, not “live”.
Noun after “of”
Use the plural form because it’s one among many friends → “friends”, not “friend”.
Putting it together
One (singular) of my friends (plural) lives (singular verb) in Brighton.
❌ Why the others are wrong:
B → “friend” (wrong; should be plural)
C → “live” (wrong verb; should be singular “lives”)
D → both noun and verb are wrong

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: One of my best friend is getting married today
One of my best friends are getting married today
One of my best friends is getting married today
One of my best friend is getting marry today
questions.explanation:
“One of the …” structure
The subject is “one”, which is singular, so the verb must also be singular → “is”.
Noun after “of”
Use the plural form because it’s one among many best friends → “friends”, not “friend”.
Verb form “getting married”
The correct expression is “getting married”, not “getting marry”.
Putting it together
One (singular) of my best friends (plural) is getting married today.
❌ Why the others are wrong:
A → “friend” (wrong; should be plural)
B → “are” (wrong verb; should be singular “is”)
D → “friend” + “getting marry” (both wrong)

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: One of my bags were stolen from the shop
One of my bags was stolen from the shop
One of my bag were stolen from the shop
One of my bag was stolen from the shop
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Subject-verb agreement:
The main subject is “One” (singular), even though it is followed by “of my bags” (plural).
Singular subject → singular verb → “was”.
Plural possession:
“Bags” is plural because you own more than one bag.
So the correct sentence is:
One of my bags was stolen from the shop.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. One of my bags were stolen… → “were” is plural, but subject One is singular → wrong.
C. One of my bag were stolen… → “bag” is singular, but should be plural to match “one of my ___” → also verb “were” is wrong.
D. One of my bag was stolen… → “bag” should be plural → “bags”.

questions.question:
One of the major ----- 
load-shedding.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
One of the major ___ load-shedding.
“One of the …” → The main subject is One (singular).
Noun choice: “problem” is singular to match “One,” even though it’s part of “major problems”.
So the correct sentence is:
One of the major problems is load-shedding.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. problems are → “problems” is plural, but “One of the …” is singular → verb must be singular.
C. problems is → “problems” is plural, cannot pair with singular verb correctly.
D. problematic issues are → grammatically odd and wordy; “issues” is plural → verb mismatch.

questions.question: Last year, one of the major ----- load shedding.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Last year, one of the major load shedding ___.
“One of the …” → The main subject is One (singular).
Tense: “Last year” → past tense → verb should be was.
Noun choice: “problem” is singular to match “One.”
So the correct sentence is:
Last year, one of the major problems was load shedding.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. problems is → Present tense “is” is wrong; “problems” is plural → mismatch.
C. problems was → Plural noun “problems” with singular “One” → mismatch.
D. problems has been → Present perfect tense does not match “Last year” (past time reference) and plural noun is wrong.

questions.question: One should obey ----- parents.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
One should obey ___ parents.
The pronoun “One” is formal and indefinite.
To match “One”, we must use the corresponding possessive pronoun: “one’s”.
So the correct sentence is:
One should obey one’s parents.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. his → Could be used in informal or traditional English, but the sentence uses “One”, so formal grammar prefers one’s.
B. your → Changes the subject from general “one” to “you” → grammatically incorrect.
C. their → Plural or gender-neutral, does not match singular “one.”

questions.question: Find out the correct sentence.[]
options: One should not give opinion unasked
One should not give one's opinion unasked
One should not deliver his opinion unasked
One should not give his opinion unasked
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
Subject: The sentence uses “One” → formal, indefinite pronoun.
Possessive: To match “One”, we must use “one’s” (not “his” or “his/her”).
Verb phrase: “give one’s opinion” is the correct formal English expression.
So the correct sentence is:
One should not give one's opinion unasked.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. One should not give opinion unasked → Missing possessive pronoun “one’s.”
C. One should not deliver his opinion unasked → “his” does not match formal “One,” and “deliver opinion” is awkward; we usually say give an opinion.
D. One should not give his opinion unasked → Same issue: “his” mismatches “One.”

questions.question: The more hemoglobin one has, the more oxygen is carried to ----- cells.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
The more hemoglobin one has, the more oxygen is carried to ___ cells.
The subject is “one” → formal, indefinite pronoun.
To show possession (the cells belonging to “one”), we use “one’s”.
So the correct sentence is:
The more hemoglobin one has, the more oxygen is carried to one's cells.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. its → Refers to an object or thing, not a person.
B. our → Changes the subject to first person plural → incorrect.
C. their → Plural or gender-neutral, does not match singular “one.”

questions.question: One should be careful about ----- duty.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
One should be careful about ___ duty.
The subject is “One” → formal, indefinite pronoun.
To indicate possession (the duty belonging to “one”), we use “one’s”.
So the correct sentence is:
One should be careful about one's duty.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. her → Changes the subject to female → does not match “One.”
B. his → Informal/traditional, but formal grammar prefers one’s with “One.”
C. the → “the duty” is too general; we want possession.

questions.question: One must follow ----- conscience.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
One must follow ___ conscience.
The subject is “One” → formal, indefinite pronoun.
To show possession (the conscience belonging to “one”), we use “one’s”.
So the correct sentence is:
One must follow one's conscience.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. individual's → Grammatically correct, but the sentence uses “One” → need matching pronoun.
C. right → Not a possessive pronoun → wrong.
D. personal → Adjective only; does not match the pronoun structure.

questions.question: Carl was one of the most intelligent ----- class.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Carl was one of the most intelligent ___ class.
“One of the …” → The main subject is singular (one) but it refers to a group of people.
The noun we are referring to is students → plural, because Carl is one among many students.
To show possession (belonging to “his class”), we use “of his.”
So the correct sentence is:
Carl was one of the most intelligent students of his class.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. student of their → “student” singular doesn’t match “one of the most intelligent …” and “their” is wrong for Carl (male).
B. student of his → “student” singular is incorrect; should be plural students.
D. students of their → “their” is wrong; Carl is male → “his” is correct.

questions.question:
Everyone should respect
 ----- parents.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Everyone should respect ___ parents.
“Everyone” is an indefinite singular pronoun.
In traditional/formal grammar, “his” is used as the corresponding possessive pronoun for singular indefinite subjects like “everyone.”
So the correct sentence is:
Everyone should respect his parents.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. one's → “One” and “Everyone” are different pronouns; “one’s” is incorrect here.
C. their → Modern English sometimes allows “their” as singular, but formal grammar prefers his.
D. our → Changes the subject to plural first person → incorrect.

questions.question: A student should be careful about ----- duty.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
A student should be careful about ___ duty.
“A student” is singular.
The possessive pronoun matching a singular noun like “student” in formal English is “his” (traditionally).
So the correct sentence is:
A student should be careful about his duty.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. one's → “One’s” is used with the pronoun “One”, not “a student.”
C. all → Does not show possession → grammatically incorrect.
D. the → General article; we want possession, not just “the duty.”

questions.question: Whom did you meet yesterday ? The word 'whom' is ----- pronoun.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
In the sentence:
“Whom did you meet yesterday?”
The word “whom” is used to ask a question, so it is an interrogative pronoun.
Interrogative pronouns are used to ask questions.
Examples: who, whom, whose, which, what

questions.question: Which one is the relative pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
A relative pronoun is a pronoun that introduces a relative clause and relates it to a noun mentioned before.
Common relative pronouns are:
who, whom, whose, which, that
Now look at the options:
A. He → Personal pronoun
B. You → Personal pronoun
C. His → Possessive pronoun
D. Who → ✅ Relative pronoun

questions.question: Who', 'What' and 'Which' are --- pronouns.[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
Who, what, and which can function as relative pronouns when they introduce a clause and relate it to a noun or idea mentioned before.
Common relative pronouns:
who
whom
whose
which
that

questions.question: On which type of sentences a relative pronoun joins two clauses ?[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
A relative pronoun (who, which, that, etc.) joins a subordinate clause to a main clause.
A sentence that has:
One main clause
One or more subordinate clauses
is called a complex sentence

questions.question:
In the sentence, 'I know the man who has done this'.
The word 'who' is which pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
In the sentence:
I know the man who has done this.
The word "who" introduces the clause "who has done this" and gives more information about "the man".
So, "who" is a relative pronoun because:
It refers back to the noun "man"
It joins the relative clause to the main clause
Why others are incorrect?
A. Demonstrative → this, that, these, those
C. Reflexive → myself, yourself, himself, etc.
D. Reciprocal → each other, one another

questions.question:
It is I 'who' am to blame. The word 'who' is which 
pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
In the sentence:
It is I who am to blame.
The word "who":
Refers back to "I"
Introduces the clause "who am to blame"
Connects this clause to the main clause
This is exactly what a relative pronoun does: it links a subordinate (relative) clause to a main clause and refers to a noun or pronoun.
Why others are wrong:
A. Interrogative → used to ask questions (who, what, which… in questions)
B. Demonstrative → this, that, these, those
D. Distributive → each, every, either, neither

questions.question: Who is the man that came to you ? Here 'that' is a/an ---[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
In the sentence:
Who is the man that came to you?
The word "that":
Refers back to "the man"
Introduces the clause "that came to you"
Connects this clause to the main clause
This is exactly the function of a relative pronoun.
Why others are wrong:
A. Indefinite pronoun → someone, anyone, nobody, etc.
B. Demonstrative pronoun → this, that, these, those (when pointing, not connecting clauses)
C. Interrogative pronoun → who, what, which used to ask questions

questions.question: The word 'that' is which pronoun ?[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
The word “that” can be used as different types of pronouns, but in this question, it is used as a relative pronoun.
A relative pronoun joins two clauses and refers back to a noun mentioned before it.
For example:
This is the book that I bought.
Here, “that” relates to “the book” and connects the two parts of the sentence.

questions.question: Which of the following has not used relative pronoun ?[]
options: I like people who smile a lot
There is a programme tonight which you might like
Those who want tickets can get them from the office
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
A relative pronoun connects a clause to a noun and gives more information about it (e.g., who, which, that).
Let’s check each option:
A. I like people who smile a lot.
→ “who” connects the clause smile a lot to people.
✔ Relative pronoun
B. There is a programme tonight which you might like.
→ “which” refers to programme.
✔ Relative pronoun
C. Which book do you like?
→ Here “which” is asking a question.
❌ It is an interrogative pronoun, not a relative pronoun.
D. Those who want tickets can get them from the office.
→ “who” refers to those.
✔ Relative pronoun

questions.question: Who, Which, What are ---[]
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
Who, Which, What are commonly used as relative pronouns when they connect a clause to a noun.
Examples:
The man who came here is my uncle.
The book which I bought is interesting.
I don’t know what he wants.
In these sentences, the words who, which, what introduce a clause and relate it to something mentioned earlier.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: The boy was short who snatched my hand bag
The boy snatched my hand bag who was short
The boy who snatched my hand bag was short
The boy was short who was snatching my hand bag
questions.explanation:
✅ Explanation:
In English, a relative clause should come immediately after the noun it describes.
Let’s check the options:
A. The boy was short who snatched my hand bag
❌ The relative clause “who snatched my hand bag” is placed wrongly.
B. The boy snatched my hand bag who was short
❌ The clause “who was short” is incorrectly placed. It should describe “the boy” directly.
C. The boy who snatched my hand bag was short
✔ Correct structure.
Here, “who snatched my hand bag” properly describes “the boy.”
D. The boy was short who was snatching my hand bag
❌ Incorrect structure and tense usage.

questions.question: Select the correct sentence[]
options: The man was tall who came to my office
The man came to my office who was tall
The man who came to my office was tall
My office who came was tall
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
This sentence uses a relative clause:
who came to my office
“Who” refers to the man (antecedent).
In English, the relative clause should directly follow the noun it describes.
The main sentence: The man … was tall.
So the correct structure is:
The man who came to my office was tall.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. The man was tall who came to my office → Relative clause comes after the adjective → grammatically wrong.
B. The man came to my office who was tall → Relative clause comes after the verb phrase, not immediately after the noun → confusing and wrong.
D. My office who came was tall → “My office” cannot be the antecedent of “who” → incorrect.

questions.question: Which one is correct ?[]
options: The man was tall who stole my bag
The man stole my bag who is tall
The man stole my bag who was tall
The man who stole my bag was tall
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
This sentence also uses a relative clause:
who stole my bag
“Who” refers to the man (antecedent).
The relative clause must immediately follow the noun it describes.
The main sentence: The man … was tall.
So the correct sentence is:
The man who stole my bag was tall.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. The man was tall who stole my bag → Relative clause comes after the adjective → incorrect placement.
B. The man stole my bag who is tall → Relative clause comes after the verb phrase, not after the noun → confusing.
C. The man stole my bag who was tall → Same problem → “who” should follow “the man,” not “bag.”

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: The man that said that was a fool
The man whom said that was a fool
The man who said that was a fool
The man which said was a fool
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
This sentence uses a relative clause:
who said that
“Who” refers to the man (antecedent).
“Who” is used for people as the subject of the relative clause.
The main sentence: The man … was a fool.
So the correct sentence is:
The man who said that was a fool.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. The man that said that was a fool → “That” can sometimes refer to people in informal English, but in standard grammar for people, “who” is correct.
B. The man whom said that was a fool → “Whom” is for the object of a verb, but here “who” is the subject of “said.”
D. The man which said was a fool → “Which” is used for things or animals, not people.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence[]
options: It is I who is to blame
It is I who am to blame
It is I who are to blame
It is me who are to blame
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
It is I who ___ to blame.
The relative clause “who am to blame” refers back to I.
Since the subject of the relative clause is I, the correct verb is am.
So the correct sentence is:
It is I who am to blame.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. It is I who is to blame → “is” would be used for he/she/it, not I.
C. It is I who are to blame → “are” is for you/we/they, not I.
D. It is me who are to blame → “me” is incorrect in formal grammar; should be I, and “are” is also wrong.

questions.question: I don't like stories ----- have unhappy endings.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
I don't like stories ___ have unhappy endings.
We need a relative pronoun to introduce the clause “___ have unhappy endings”.
“Stories” is plural and inanimate, so the correct relative pronoun is that (or sometimes “which”).
So the correct sentence is:
I don't like stories that have unhappy endings.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. they → “They” is a subject pronoun, not a relative pronoun.
C. whom → Used for people as the object of a verb → wrong here.
D. who → Used for people, but “stories” are not people → incorrect.

questions.question: The registered parcel ----- arrived for you is on the table.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
The registered parcel ___ arrived for you is on the table.
The noun “parcel” is an inanimate thing, not a person.
To introduce a relative clause describing a thing, we use “which.”
So the correct sentence is:
The registered parcel which arrived for you is on the table.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. who → Used for people → incorrect.
B. whom → Used for people as the object of a verb → incorrect.
D. when → Refers to time → does not fit here.

questions.question: Tell me ----- that.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Tell me ___ .
We are asking about a person who did the action.
The correct relative/interrogative pronoun for a person as the subject is who.
So the correct sentence is:
Tell me who told you.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. whom told you → “Whom” is used as object, but here it is the subject of “told.”
B. that told you → “That” can sometimes refer to people, but in standard English “who” is preferred for people.
D. told you → Missing subject → grammatically incomplete.

questions.question: This is the person ----- came the last week.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
This is the person ___ came the last week.
The noun “person” refers to a human, so we need a relative pronoun for people.
The person is the subject of the verb “came”, so the correct relative pronoun is who.
So the correct sentence is:
This is the person who came the last week.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. which → Used for things, not people → incorrect.
B. that → Can refer to people in informal English, but standard formal grammar prefers who for people.
C. whom → Used as the object of a verb or preposition, but here the person is the subject → incorrect

questions.question: The teachers ----- challenge us are the ones we remember.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
The teachers ___ challenge us are the ones we remember.
“Teachers” are people, so we need a relative pronoun referring to people.
The teachers are the subject of the verb “challenge”, so the correct pronoun is who.
So the correct sentence is:
The teachers who challenge us are the ones we remember.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. which → Refers to things, not people → incorrect.
B. whose → Shows possession → incorrect here.
C. whom → Refers to the object of a verb, but teachers are the subject → incorrect.

questions.question: The old man ----- lives next door has bought a car.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
The old man ___ lives next door has bought a car.
“Old man” is a person, so we need a relative pronoun for a human.
The old man is the subject of the verb “lives”, so the correct pronoun is who.
So the correct sentence is:
The old man who lives next door has bought a car.
❌ Why others are wrong:
B. whom → Used for the object of a verb, but “old man” is the subject → incorrect.
C. whose → Shows possession, but the sentence is about who lives next → incorrect.
D. which → Refers to things, not people → incorrect.

questions.question: Give the clothes to ----- needs them.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Give the clothes to ___ needs them.
The blank refers to the object of the preposition “to”, but within its own clause, the pronoun is the subject of the verb “needs.”
When the pronoun is the subject of its clause, we use “whoever.”
So the correct sentence is:
Give the clothes to whoever needs them.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. who → Could work for simple clauses, but in this indefinite relative clause, formal usage prefers whoever.
B. whomever → Used for objects of verbs/prepositions, but here the pronoun is the subject of “needs”” → incorrect.
D. whom → Object pronoun → incorrect.

questions.question: Choose the correct option[]
options: Give the work to whichever looks idle.
Give the work to whom looks idle.
Give the work to whomsoever looks idle.
Give the work to whoever looks idle.
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
Give the work to ___ looks idle.
The blank refers to the object of the preposition “to”, but it also functions as the subject of the relative clause “___ looks idle”.
“Whoever” is used when the pronoun is the subject of the verb in its own clause, even if it’s the object of the main sentence.
So the correct sentence is:
Give the work to whoever looks idle.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. whichever looks idle → “Whichever” is used for things, not people → incorrect.
B. whom looks idle → “Whom” is for objects, but here it’s the subject of the clause “looks idle”” → incorrect.
C. whomsoever looks idle → Same problem → clause requires subject, not object → incorrect.

questions.question: You can discuss the issue with ----- you feel can solve your problem.[]
questions.explanation:
Explanation:
The sentence is:
You can discuss the issue with ___ you feel can solve your problem.
The blank refers to the object of the preposition “with”, not the subject.
“Whomever” is the correct relative pronoun for the object of a verb or preposition.
So the correct sentence is:
You can discuss the issue with whomever you feel can solve your problem.
❌ Why others are wrong:
A. who → Used for the subject, but here the person is the object of “with” → incorrect.
B. whom → Would work in simple cases, but with “you feel can solve your problem”, the clause is a complex one → we use whomever.
C. whoever → Refers to the subject of a clause → incorrect in this sentence.
